title: Headlines: Jetstar class action update
transcript:
Speaker 1: This episode is sponsored by our friends over at Tourism Tasmania.
Speaker 2: From the Daily Os, I'm Emma Golespi.
Speaker 1: I'm Adela Bianini.
Speaker 2: It's Monday, the 23rd of November.
Speaker 1: Here's what's making headlines this evening.
Speaker 2: More than a million Jetstar customers are being contacted about a class action lawsuit against the airline.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the budget carrier cancelled flights and gave affected customers vouchers.
In 2024, law firm Echo Law filed a class action in the Federal Court, alleging Jetstar should have offered refunds instead, breaching its own rules and its obligations under the Australian Consumer Law.
In October, Echo Law amended his claim, drawing on Jetstar's internal documents, alleging the airline knowingly misled customers about their right to a refund.
Jetstar denies the allegations.
A spokesperson said customers were offered, quote, " travel credits, fee-free flight changes and refunds," and that COVID vouchers have had no expiry date since 2023.
Qantas, which owns Jetstar, agreed to pay $105 million to settle a similar class action in March this year.
The deal is awaiting approval in the Federal Court.
Speaker 1: Small businesses will be exempt from the federal government's plans for online safety crackdowns.
Communications Minister Anika Wells confirmed the carve-out on Monday as Labour pushes to pass its digital duty of care legislation in the final sitting week of the year.
Wells said the bill's intention was to quote "put the onus on tech companies to protect Australians from online harms before they occur," not to create additional burden for low-risk small businesses.
With the coalition opposed, Labour needs the Greens support in the Senate.
The minor party wants individuals to be able to sue Big Tech and tougher action on hate speech based on race, sexuality, disability, and gender.
Greens communication spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said she was optimistic a deal could be reached.
Speaker 2: A rumored Chinese spy at the heart of Nvidia's recent scandal was reportedly in touch with Chinese agencies during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang.
The New York Times has reported Alice Huang was in contact with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security for over 12 months between 2025 and 2026.
Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Mega Speed International and imported Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions in Nvidia chip sales.
US authorities have been investigating Mega Speed since 2024 over concerns it smuggled Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.
Trump administration officials have repeatedly said they have not concluded that Alice Huang spied for China.
Speaker 1: And today's good news, a 128-year-old maritime mystery has been solved with the discovery of a 16 meter gunboat off the coast of Far North Queensland.
The Ex-HMCS Spitfire launched in 1855 as the first warship commissioned for service by the Australian government.
It was sold into private ownership in 1885 as a fishing vessel.
The Spitfire went down in tropical waters of Far North Queensland in 1898 with no loss of life, but its final resting place was unknown until the 21st of August this year when maritime archaeologists located the wreck after a month-long expedition.
James Hunter from the Australian National Maritime Museum said the fact that Spitfire outlasted most sailing vessels of its era was a testament to the quality of its design and construction.
Speaker 2: That's the latest from the Daily Oz newsroom.
If you're looking for something else, you can catch up on this morning's deep dive on the debate over the four-day working week.
Speaker 1: We'll be back tomorrow with another deep dive, but until then, have a good one.
